sections.body:
Modesty concerns restraint in claiming status, importance, superiority, or special credit. It is not low self-esteem, low ability, lack of ambition, virtue, invisibility, or refusal to describe real contributions.

“Modesty within Agreeableness: restraint in self-presentation and status claims” is used on this page as a descriptive construct within the NEO/IPIP-NEO 30-facet framework. The official IPIP resource describes scales that measure constructs similar to NEO facets and lists item mappings ([S11](https://ipip.ori.org/Finding_Scales_to_Measure_Particular_Constructs.htm)); this does not make scores from different instruments, translations, or products interchangeable.

FermatMind has not published product-level reliability, validity, Chinese norms, or individual predictive evidence for the score discussed on this page. This material is for self-observation and education. It is not for clinical diagnosis, hiring screening, school admission, or replacing a career decision.

> **Content method and update:** FermatMind Editorial prepared this page with AI-assisted drafting and checked terminology, boundaries, and evidence against public personality-psychology sources. It is for self-understanding and education; it is not clinical diagnosis, hiring screening, or individual-outcome prediction. Substantive update: 2026-07-19; review mode: solo_operator; not clinically reviewed.
sections.heading: Evidence and Interpretation Boundaries

sections.body: A stronger tendency may downplay distinction and emphasize collective contribution. A weaker tendency may state achievements and status more readily. Accuracy, fairness, audience, and cultural context determine whether either presentation is useful.
sections.heading: Precise Definition

sections.body: Modesty belongs to [Agreeableness](/en/personality/big-five/agreeableness), reflecting how status is presented in interpersonal space.
sections.heading: Parent Domain

sections.body:
- **Modesty versus self-esteem:** Internal evaluation and public presentation are different.
- **Modesty versus Achievement Striving:** Ambition can be strong while self-promotion remains restrained.
- **Modesty versus honesty:** Underclaiming can be as inaccurate as exaggeration.
sections.heading: Distinguishing Neighboring Facets

sections.body: Stronger Modesty may appear as redirecting praise, avoiding status display, or using “we” for shared work. Weaker tendency may appear as naming accomplishments, negotiating visibility, or enjoying recognition. Culture, gender norms, discrimination, and job incentives strongly affect consequences.
sections.heading: Behavioral Cues

sections.body: A person may be modest socially and precise in a résumé. Some environments punish self-promotion; others make invisible work easy to overlook. Observed style does not establish inner worth.
sections.heading: Contextual Differences

sections.body:
- Sharing credit readily.
- Avoiding superiority claims.
- Keeping accomplishments private.
- Losing opportunities because evidence is omitted.
- Downplaying expertise that others need to identify.
sections.heading: Possible Expressions When Stronger

sections.body:
- Naming achievements and status directly.
- Advocating for recognition.
- Making contribution legible.
- Claiming disproportionate credit.
- Turning comparison into a recurring interaction.
sections.heading: Possible Expressions When Weaker

sections.body: Stronger Modesty can support shared status and reduce competition. Possible costs include underrecognition and inaccurate self-presentation. Weaker Modesty can support visibility and negotiation; possible costs include boastfulness or credit conflict. Neither level measures worth.
sections.heading: Strengths and Costs

sections.body: A researcher describes her exact contribution, credits collaborators, and provides evidence in an interview. Accurate self-advocacy does not require abandoning Modesty.
sections.heading: An Original Case

sections.body: A frequent self-promoter privately doubts his value. Visible status claims do not establish high self-esteem.
sections.heading: An Original Counterexample

sections.body:
1. Do you describe contributions accurately or minimize them?
2. How do you divide shared credit?
3. Which audience needs evidence of your work?
4. When does recognition become comparison?
5. Which cultural rules shape your self-presentation?
sections.heading: Self-Observation Questions

sections.body: Write a three-sentence account of one contribution: action, evidence, and collaborator credit. Practice saying it without apology or inflation.
sections.heading: Low-Risk Action Experiment

sections.body: Return to [Agreeableness](/en/personality/big-five/agreeableness) or the [30-facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets). Continue with [Trust](/en/personality/big-five/facets/trust), [Straightforwardness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/straightforwardness), [Altruism](/en/personality/big-five/facets/altruism), [Compliance](/en/personality/big-five/facets/compliance), [Tender-Mindedness](/en/personality/big-five/facets/tender-mindedness).
